About me

Born and raised in Peru, I saw early how much design quietly assumes about a person: their connection, their device, their time, their margin for error. I build for everyone, especially the people those assumptions leave out.

How I work

Systems thinking

Case study 01 · ServiceNow

AI Cockpit.

Helping support managers see what needs them first.

RolePrincipal Product Designer,
sole designer
Partners1 PM · 1 Engineering lead ·
UX Research
Approvers11 stakeholders
TimeframeJoined April 2026 ·
ongoing

Context · What I walked into

I joined ServiceNow, and this project, in April 2026 as the sole designer. Engineering was already building toward a July ship date.

Inherited

A working engineering proof of concept

A ship date

A functional spec

Missing

Research

A defined user

Success measures

A design point of view in the room

Problem

Every shift starts by reconstructing the night. One manager opens 100+ emails a morning, around 70 of them P1 alerts, to find the few that need a response.

The loud already surfaces. Engineers ping their manager the moment something breaks.

The quiet does not. A case goes stale, a customer waits, an engineer hits capacity and says nothing.

More alerts make it worse. Managers already get more than they can read.

Managers rarely miss an emergency. They miss the slow drift that no alert catches.

Research · In their words

“It’s a bit labor intensive. I’m looking for the diamonds in the rough. What do I actually need to do?”

CS Admin Manager · APJ

“What’s gone ignored the longest, and what’s yelling at me the loudest. If I can look at those two, I can prioritize my day.”

Support Delivery Manager · EMEA

Research · What it found

I joined with no research to inherit, so I ran it. Five managers and two stakeholders, across the US, APJ, and EMEA.

A UX researcher recruited participants and sat in, co-leading two sessions and owning the jobs-to-be-done. I planned the sessions, wrote the loose guide, ran synthesis, and produced the day-in-the-life journey, the user flow, task analysis, user requirements, and the persona.

01

Context before action

Managers act on understanding, not numbers. They want to know why before they decide what to do.

02

The quiet drift is the real risk

Urgent cases surface on their own. Stale cases, unanswered customers, and overloaded engineers stay invisible.

03

They live in chat

Most coordination happens in Teams, not a dashboard.

04

They already built their own fixes

Every manager had a workaround. The need is real, and adoption of anything new is not guaranteed.

Research · The shape of a day

Seven tools before the first decision. I mapped a manager’s full day, from shift start through handover.

JOURNEY ARTIFACTDay-in-the-life map across Teams, email, dashboards, case records, and calls, from shift start to handover. Annotated with where the quiet drift hides.

Design framing

The challenge

How might we bring the right signal to managers at the right moment, so they can act before things escalate?

The principles
01

Replace something

Every new surface has to earn its place by removing one.

02

Show the loud and the quiet

Surface the urgent and the slow drift in the same view.

03

Connect across tools and team

One read of the moment, from every signal a manager tracks today.

04

Make verifying instant

One tap to wherever the signal came from.

05

Adapt to the moment

Shift start, mid-shift, and handover each need something different.

Strategic pivot · Two directions

Ambient Intelligence Command Center Who movesSignal comes to the managerManager goes to the signal Where it livesTeams, Outlook, wherever they workOne page in the Support portal Adoption riskLower: fits existing behaviorHigher: asks for a new habit Build complexityHigher: multi-surfaceLower: single surface

Both are grounded in the research. I reframed the choice for the team: not which one to build, but in what order to build them.

Strategic pivot · The concepts

I designed both directions far enough to make the tradeoffs real.

CONCEPT A · VIDEOAmbient Intelligence: morning briefing in Teams, a mid-shift nudge, a handover summary in context

Ambient Intelligence

CONCEPT B · VIDEOCommand Center: At Risk, Attention Signals, and Workload in one Support portal page

Command Center

Strategic pivot · The decision

I changed the question: not which one, but in what order.

Research pointed to Ambient as the better experience. Engineering had started the simpler dashboard, and there was a July date. Ambient is multi-surface. It could not ship by July. Pushing it outright would have cost the date, and the room.

I made the tradeoffs explicit. Ambient wins on adoption. The dashboard wins on time and risk. Both are true. So I proposed a sequence, not a winner: ship the dashboard as the MVP, designed as the foundation of the ambient system, then earn the rest.

Eleven approving stakeholders, no mandate, and no team of my own. The alignment came from making the path legible, not from authority.

The work · Phased plan

One sequence: the MVP ships on the inherited date, and every phase builds toward the ambient promise.

Reflection · What I carry forward

01

The vacuum fills with whoever is in the room

Joining mid-build, design’s seat is not granted. I claimed it with evidence: research and success measures, locked in the first week.

02

A real choice beats a strong opinion

Two concepts grounded in user truth moved the debate off preference and onto tradeoffs.

03

Sequencing dissolved the conflict

The MVP and the vision stopped competing the moment I ordered them. The dashboard became the first step of the Ambient plan instead of its rival.

04

What I would do differently

Bring the business owner into the research itself, not just the readouts. She arrived with a fixed answer, and the push and pull with design and research continues today. Findings move people fastest when they helped discover them.

Case study 02 · Walmart

Project Phoenix.

Rescuing item setup for a marketplace of 180K+ sellers.

RolePrincipal UX Designer
Team3 PM · 11 Eng · 2 Content ·
2 designers I led
TimeframeFeb 2024 to Jan 2025

Context · What I walked into

Seller Center looked like one product. Underneath, it was nine platforms, nine sets of rules, nine dead ends.

The seller’s reality

A seller could list an item, wait hours, and get back an error code they could not read, with no way to fix it. The patterns nobody questioned were the ones causing the most pain.

The design reality

Design had been a production role here for years. Junior designers were doing their best without a systems background. Senior designers had stopped seeing the seams. I brought a systems lens the team had not had room to apply: we started designing the foundation, not just the next ticket.

Problem · What sellers faced

The catalog sellers faced: errors, drafts, and statuses, with no guidance on what to do next.

Research · The finding

The items that errored most were the ones sellers had no way to diagnose. Every error code was written for engineers. Sellers were guessing.

An item could flip from Pass to Error with no action from the seller. No diagnosis and no path to recover: just edit, resubmit, wait hours, and read the next code.

Design framing · The approach

Two tracks at once: ship relief now, build the case for the real fix.

01

Make 200+ errors legible

The short-term fix: I translated the error codes into plain language, each with a priority and a path to recover. The long-term question: why were they firing at all, and why did even a translated error leave sellers stuck? That question spun off the Item Error Resolution track.

02

Trace the system behind the symptom

Inside that track I followed one item across five systems. Each validation checkpoint fired its own errors and pushed its own passing states to the UI, each labeled differently. Items flipped from Pass to Error while sellers had done nothing.

03

Standardize what every team rebuilds

The GTIN patch was helper text on a text box. Looking across the journey, three other teams were building their own GTIN validation flows at that moment, all similar, all different. I standardized input and validation into one accessible design-system component.

04

Turn quick fixes into evidence

17 fixes, each shipped in five business days or less, each logged: the problem, the patch, the system flaw it pointed to. The log became the business case for the foundation work.

The approach · Where items break

One item, five systems. The trace showed exactly where sellers got trapped, and what they should have seen instead.

ARTIFACT 01 · BACKENDThe item moving across five backend validation checkpoints, each firing its own states

ARTIFACT 02 · FRONTENDThe same path with no backend layer exposed: one streamlined flow for the seller

The work · Beyond the screens

Phoenix also changed how we work together.

01

A formal Design QA step

A shared checkpoint between UX and engineering, so what ships matches what was designed.

02

A brief built for designers

A v-team of principal designers and the Operations PM lead set out to redesign the PM-owned PRD; the pilot stalled. So I reframed it as a Design brief, owned by design, holding everything we need to understand a problem: prior work, success metrics, timelines.

03

Inclusive design, operationalized

With the Accessibility team in the International Design org, I wrote inclusive and accessibility guidelines and an operating procedure for Seller Center designers.

04

Designers who think in systems

I brought two designers onto the short-term fixes and coached them to think at the system level. They grew into the long-term tracks with me; one carried a series of reporting projects.

“Jenny consistently integrates business and seller needs into her designs and has delivered significant results with the Phoenix work this year.”

Reflection · What I carry forward

01

Quick fixes are worth what you learn from them

Each patch was logged: the problem, the fix, and the system flaw it pointed to. The log, not the patches, is what won the investment in the foundation.

02

Patterns travel further than screens

The GTIN component, the confirmation messages, and the design brief each landed in every business unit. Designing with Supplier, Merchant, and Ads, not just for my team, compounded the impact.

03

What I would do differently

See the pattern in the patches sooner. My manager asked me to log the quick fixes so we would not lose the backlog. As the log grew, and as other designers described their own problem spaces in crits and office hours, the overlapping themes appeared. Next time, the log starts on day one.

The recurring pattern

In both projects, the ask on the surface hid the real problem.

At ServiceNow, the brief was a smarter alert. The real problem was the quiet drift no one could see.

At Walmart, the ask was patches. The real problem was a platform with no shared logic.

Every time, I start with the same question: what are we actually solving? That question is where the strategy comes from. It is also where the design comes from.
